analysis.one_liner: Counts hospital observation stays toward Medicare's three-day rule for nursing home coverage.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Medicare fix with 24 cosponsors, including Republicans, died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare, a hospital stay only counts toward skilled nursing facility coverage if the patient is officially an 'inpatient' for three days. Hospitals increasingly label seniors 'outpatient observation' instead — even when they spend a week in a hospital bed — which strips those days from the count and leaves patients owing the full cost of nursing home care, often more than $10,000. This bill would simply count observation days toward the three-day requirement, restoring coverage for patients whose care was real but mislabeled.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who spend days in the hospital under observation status and then need skilled nursing care. They would keep Medicare's nursing home coverage instead of paying thousands of dollars out of pocket for care they assumed was covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors stuck with observation-status nursing home bills

how_it_helps.text: Counts time spent under outpatient observation status toward Medicare's three-day inpatient hospital requirement, so those patients qualify for covered skilled nursing facility care [S3].

Protects patients from unexpected nursing home bills averaging more than $10,000 out of pocket for stays Medicare refused to cover, according to the HHS Office of Inspector General as cited in the bill's findings [S3].
Applies retroactively to services beginning January 1, 2015, including completed stays where an appeal is filed within 90 days of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare, and ultimately taxpayers, would pay the cost of nursing home stays that previously fell on patients. Hospitals would also face no new mandate but lose a billing practice that shifts costs onto patients and deters them from pressing hospitals on admission status.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare, taxpayers, and hospitals' billing flexibility

drawbacks.text: The bill raises federal Medicare spending, since the government rather than the patient absorbs nursing home costs for observation-status patients; the bill text does not include an offset to pay for this [S3].

It does not fix the underlying incentive: hospitals would still be free to classify patients as outpatient observation, a practice that grew sharply — outpatient visits up 28.5% while inpatient stays fell 12.6% between 2006 and 2012 — because observation status shields hospitals from billing scrutiny, and the bill leaves that choice untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the affected patients, the benefit is straightforward and large: coverage they already earned in a hospital bed, instead of a five-figure bill. The honest cost is higher federal Medicare spending with no dedicated offset, and the bill treats the symptom — the patient's penalty — without stopping hospitals from continuing to use observation status in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 24, 2015 by Sen. Sherrod Brown with original cosponsors including Republicans Susan Collins and Shelley Moore Capito, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, and no Senate floor action in the 114th Congress [S5].
It drew 24 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 4 Republicans, bipartisan support that never translated into committee action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Medicare program's finances, and hospitals that kept the flexibility to classify patients as outpatient observation without losing the cost shift onto patients and their families.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare's balance sheet and hospitals' billing flexibility

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan cosponsors

for.name: Sens. Susan Collins, Bill Nelson, and Shelley Moore Capito

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 20 Democrats and 4 Republicans cosponsored, with Republicans Collins and Capito among the original four — and the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: Observation status shields hospitals from admission-review scrutiny while shifting five-figure nursing home bills onto patients; the bill would strip the patient-penalty side of that arrangement without restricting hospitals' ability to keep classifying patients as outpatients. Hospitals lose a cost shift but keep the classification flexibility.
More patients would have their nursing home stays covered by Medicare instead of paying privately or going without care. Facilities get paid for care they currently provide unpaid or forgo.

Medicare would absorb nursing home costs it currently pushes onto patients, with no dedicated offset in the bill. In budget terms a loss, but it is a cost transferred from individual families to the shared insurance pool.
